title: Remove the motor bodily-injury IBNER lift (D-11), or at least stop lifting closed claims; settle the 2025 motor level on that basis (absorbs the #151 level-correction proposal)
gain_2023: These are proxy figures, not a refit. I modelled a D-11-off refit as the production backtest mu x 0.940, which is the shift that taking out the 2022 lift makes to a log-linear year trend fitted on 2021-22 and projected to 2023. Scored against the no-lift yardstick (y_noI, rebuilt claim by claim): +0.00059 motor D2 on all rows, +0.00238 without the 11.89m row. Scored against the production lifted yardstick (y_full): -0.00097 on all rows, +0.00098 without the 11.89m row.
gain_2024: Same proxy method, with mu x 0.9075 (the trend shift for 2021-23 projected to 2024). Against y_noI: +0.00097 motor D2. Against y_full: -0.00063. The 11.89m row is not in 2024. Even on its own lifted basis, production is 5.3% high in 2024 (the D2-best scale is 0.9725). Excluding the 11.89m row, it is 9.3% high in 2023 (best scale 0.92).
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. No production run with D11 apply=false appears in AUDIT_LOG (A15-A26), DECISIONS or config.json (D11 apply=true, not signed off). backtest_development.py switches it off only inside the development backtest, on both sides. A15/A16 call the lift a 'lower bound', so the pack has only ever considered it too small, never too large. The candidate is novel. The document inconsistency is confirmed: evidence/lines/ev_10_ibner_check.csv (before de-duplication) gives 1.0759 with a mean of 19,564, while the current glm_lines file gives 1.0854 with 19,392. MODEL_DOCUMENTATION 3.3 and D-11 still quote the old values. One factual correction: the 11.89m claim is OPEN (paid 0.74m), not closed, so an open-only lift would still lift it. It remains true that closed claims are lifted, because sql/10 joins ibner_factor without looking at status.
(2) Signal. I rebuilt the sql/10 bodily-injury development claim by claim in my own DuckDB session. It reproduces ev_10 exactly with the lift: 46.21 / 52.25 / 62.10 / 45.96m. Without the lift it gives 48.14m for 2022, 51.11m for 2023 and 39.87m for 2024 (the 2024 BF factor becomes 1.8984 on a prior of 219.7). Developed motor totals fall 3.4% / 8.3% / 5.2%, which matches the candidate.
I then tried to refute the premise that open bodily-injury claims are under-reserved:
(a) Q4 2022 and Q1 2023 losses have the same open share (0.361 and 0.354), yet the median falls from 13.9k to 10.2k, p75 from 27.4k to 20.5k and p90 from 46.3k to 34.7k. The closed median falls from 15.0k to 11.0k.
(b) In 2021-22 the open share rose from 0.13 to 0.36 while the median stayed between 12.4k and 14.0k, so the open share does not depress claim size.
(c) The break follows the loss date, not the report date. Claims reported in H1 2023 keep the old level if the loss was in 2022 (median 13.1k) and show the new level if it was in 2023 (10.1k). Q4 2022 losses reported in 2023 have a median of 12.9k. By month, December 2022 is 12.7k and January 2023 is 9.3k.
(d) The share of claims below the 2021-22 median moves from 0.50 to 0.595 for closed claims and to 0.62 for open claims in 2023, so it is the whole distribution that shifts (p25 falls from about 5.6k to about 4.0k).
This is a real severity change from 1 January 2023 that persists into 2024, not IBNER. Closed claims are final and show the full step. There is a weak hint of slight under-reserving of open claims: open shares sit 2-3 points above closed in 2022-23, worth perhaps +2-3% on open claims at most.
The result is not driven by one claim. Without the 11.89m row, the proxy gain is larger on both yardsticks in 2023, and 2024 does not contain it. The feature probe does not apply, because this changes the yardstick rather than adding a feature. I used a two-yardstick regret table instead.
(3) Risk.
- The two-year rule cannot judge this change. On production's own yardstick the change loses in 2024 and in 2023 on all rows, so the pack's usual test would reject it for the wrong reason.
- If the generator does under-reserve open bodily injury (the minority hypothesis), the proxy loses 0.0006-0.0010 motor D2.
- Under a real step, a single log-linear trend through it falls below the post-step level by about half the step size, roughly 3% of motor. My trend-shift calculation gives x0.924 for 2025 with one trend. A step treatment should give about x0.95-0.96, but that is a rough guess I have not computed. The step cannot be backtested in the 2021-22 window, so only the 2024 backtest can judge the step treatment.
- With the lift off, the 2024 BF prior still mixes pre-step 2022 with post-step 2023, so 2024 bodily injury remains a few per cent high (the C13 territory).
- Selection risk is low: the motivation comes from the data structure, not from tuning on backtest scores.
recommended_test:
Owner-run only, because it changes the target basis and appends to the audit log.
(1) In config.json set flags.D11_ibner_motor_bi.apply=false and run python/run_glm_lines.py with --run-label "C1 D-11 off, one trend". Change nothing else; contents and buildings are unaffected. Report the motor trend_pa (production 0.0553; I expect about 0.038), rate_2025 (production 627.4; I expect about 580 with one trend), sigma_year, the credibility k values and the large-claim tail adjustment (production 0.765).
(2) Run a second variant that adds a post-2023 indicator (yr>=2023) next to t in the motor small-claim GLM, under the same flag, so that the step is not projected forward as a trend. It is identifiable only in the 2024 backtest and the final fit; in the 2023 window, keep one trend. I expect 2025 at about x0.95-0.96 of production; this is rough and not computed.
(3) Score both refits and production against both yardsticks: y_full with D-11 on, and y_noI with D-11 off (the motor_ynoi table that <review scratch>/agents/verify-C1/build_ynoi.py rebuilds from claims.parquet). Score each with and without the 11.89m row (<review scratch>/agents/verify-C1/regret.py shows the pattern), and choose by the minimum worst-case loss.
(4) Make one leaderboard A/B that differs from the current production file only in motor, at the D-11-off level. I expect a mean per row of about 455-472 against 492.1; v014's 424.9 sits below that.
Do not also apply the A25 x0.96 development-bias scaling on top. Re-measure the development bias on the D-11-off basis in the same run, together with C13 (a post-step-only BF prior for 2024 bodily injury). Then correct MODEL_DOCUMENTATION 3.3 and D-11: 1.076 / 19,564 are pre-D-19 values, and the current figures are 1.0854 / 19,392.
reasoning:
D-11 assumes that the fall in like-for-like bodily-injury claim size comes from open-claim case reserves that will develop upwards. The data contradicts this.
- The fall is a single step at the 1 January 2023 loss-date boundary, between quarters with identical open shares (0.36).
- It appears equally in closed (final) claims and open claims, and across the whole distribution (p25 to p90 all fall by about 25%).
- It follows the loss date, not the report date.
- It persists through 2024.
- Earlier, when the open share rose from 0.13 to 0.36 in 2021-22, claim size did not fall at all.
This looks like a deliberate generator severity change, of the kind a reform would cause. It is very unlikely to reverse in 2025. D-11 therefore lifts 2022/2023/2024 bodily injury by 8.5% / 21.5% / 16.3% for something that is not IBNER. That raises developed motor by 3.4% / 8.3% / 5.2% and adds roughly 1.7 points of spurious slope to the motor trend; on my trend-shift calculation the 2025 motor rate sits about 4-8% too high.
I re-measured the stakes with a proxy regret table on the production backtest predictions, after rebuilding the development claim by claim and reproducing ev_10 exactly:
- If the D-11-off basis is right, the off-model gains about +0.0006 (2023) and +0.0010 (2024) motor D2. That is above the +0.0003 bar on both years.
- If the production basis is right, it loses about 0.0010 and 0.0006.
- Without the single 11.89m claim, the off-model wins in 2023 on both bases.
Because the data evidence strongly favours the no-lift basis, the expected gain is positive: about +0.0003 to +0.0005 pooled if motor is about half the pooled baseline deviance.
It cannot be validated by the pack's two-year rule, which scores against the lifted yardstick and would reject the change. Its gains are proxies from level-scaling, not refits, and the step-versus-trend choice adds 3-4% of uncertainty. Hence: worth testing through an owner-run D-11-off refit, a two-yardstick regret table and a single motor-only leaderboard A/B, not adopting on the strength of these numbers alone.
The candidate's small factual slip, that the 11.89m claim is closed (it is open), does not change the conclusion. The documentation figures of 1.076 and 19,564 are stale values from before de-duplication.

title: Buildings XGBoost: add engineered peril interactions x_clay_dry (clay x dry_summer_index) and x_fz3_rain (flood zone 3+ or missing x rainfall)
gain_2023: These are my own in-memory refits of the production buildings model without CANN. Trees were fixed at the baseline's 131 and predictions averaged over 4 XGBoost seeds; the baseline reproduces 0.11102 / 0.11046 at the default seed. The full candidate (C2) gains +0.00120, level-matched +0.00118, customer-bootstrap 95% interval +0.00002 to +0.00234. By seed the gain runs from +0.00096 to +0.00161. With x_clay_dry alone (3 seeds) it is +0.00059 (-0.00052 to +0.00159). With x_fz3_rain alone it is +0.00008, which is noise. The placebos are all at or below zero: two noise columns -0.00048, the C2 columns permuted -0.00018, random-address binary x weather -0.00013. Out of window, scoring 2022 (a year the finder's scan never used, with 2025-like dryness): C2 gains +0.00072 fitting 2023-24 (-0.00011 to +0.00163) and +0.00036 fitting 2021, against -0.00008 and -0.00015 for the random placebo.
gain_2024: Same set-up as 2023. C2 gains +0.00075, level-matched +0.00062, 95% interval -0.00015 to +0.00172. By seed the gain runs from +0.00018 to +0.00111; one seed of four falls below +0.0003. x_clay_dry alone gains +0.00083, level-matched +0.00083 (+0.00002 to +0.00175). x_fz3_rain alone gains +0.00007 (level-matched -0.00006), yet it raises the 2024 level by 1.2%. The placebos range from 0.0000 to +0.00019. Effect on the 2025 test total, fixed trees: C2 -0.50% and +0.02% (2 seeds); clay-only -0.94% and -0.44%. For comparison, changing only the seed moves the baseline 2025 total by 0.83%.
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. The model has no product or interaction features. A17 1b (weather-peril split, -0.0015 / -0.0018) is a different structure. A13's "depth 1 is enough" finding is about contents. C2 is not in AUDIT_LOG A01-A26, section 5.3, config.json or python/.
(2) Seed and perturbation noise. colsample_bytree is 0.8, so adding any column reshuffles the trees. On the finder's own predictions, adding C2 moved predictions by about 5-6% on rows outside clay and flood zone 3+ as well. I therefore ran 4 seeds of base, C2, two pure-noise columns and the C2 columns permuted, plus 3 seeds of a random-address binary x the same weather (a structural placebo), clay-only and fz3-only. Placebos average -0.0005 to +0.0002; C2 beats every placebo on average in both years. The production seed is also the best of four baselines on 2023 (0.11102 against 0.11025-0.11037), so single-seed comparisons favour the incumbent.
(3) Concentration. The whole gain comes from rows with claims above 20k, offset by rows with no claim. Symmetric trimming of the 200 customers with the largest contributions flips the finder's single-seed gains negative in 3 of 4 cases. That is expected for subsidence, which is large, but it means the gain is noisy.
(4) Physics in the raw data. Subsidence frequency on clay with dry_summer_index of 0.7 or more is 9.9 / 8.8 / 8.1 / 7.0 per 1,000 in 2021-24, against 1.0-1.65 everywhere else. Dryness has no effect on non-clay soils. The baseline's A/E in that cell is 1.17 (2023) and 1.36 (2024), against about 1.04 for other rows; C2 cuts it to 1.10 and 1.27. Flood frequency, by contrast, is flat in rainfall within every flood zone (for example zone 3 is 6.97 / 7.03 / 6.79 / 6.66 per 1,000 across rainfall bands). x_fz3_rain therefore has no support in the data. It adds about 0 to shape and shifts the 2024 level instead, which is a #143-type risk.
(5) Probe. Banded corrections fail: soil x dry with 5 bands gives -0.0007 / -0.0010. A single 3-cell indicator passes (+0.00085 / +0.00060), but that cell was chosen after the fact.
(6) Leak. dry_summer_index is same-year weather supplied in the 2025 test file and already a model feature, so this is not an outcome leak.
(7) Selection. The finder chose the pair after scanning about 50 pairs on 2023-24 residuals. The subsidence pattern holds in all four raw years, which mitigates this, and the 2022 out-of-window gain is positive but not significant.
recommended_test:
Primary variant: x_clay_dry only. The owner may test C2 as given as a second variant, but drop x_fz3_rain unless it adds shape on its own; it showed none.
Implementation: in sql/11_line_models.sql, in the CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE buildings_model statement, add the column CASE WHEN soil_type = 'clay' THEN dry_summer_index ELSE 0 END AS x_clay_dry. Rows with missing soil get 0. Then append "x_clay_dry" to config.json lines.models.buildings.numeric. Leave the large-claim GLM unchanged for this test; the finder's excess_clay_rain variant (+0.0004 / +0.0006) is a separate later test.
Owner runs run_glm_lines.py under the two-year rule, both with re-tuned trees and with trees fixed at 131. Because colsample_bytree 0.8 makes single-seed differences about ±0.0005, the owner should also average at least 4 xgboost.seed values for base and variant. The scratch harness <review scratch>/agents/verify-C2/verify_c2.py shows the pattern: an in-memory prepare(), cfg["xgboost"]["seed"] varied, and Line.build plus Line.predict on the tune and backtest windows.
Adopt only if the seed-averaged gain is positive on both years and the D-23 two-year customer bootstrap excludes zero. Then refit CANN on top. Check the 2025 buildings total against #143: expect between -0.9% and 0%, which is within seed noise of the total.
Expected gain: about +0.0006 to +0.0012 buildings D2 per year, roughly a third of that on a pooled Kaggle score. The structural support is strong; the measured margin is only about 1-2 standard errors per year.
reasoning:
I tried to refute C2 as noise from perturbing the trees, as selection, or as a level effect, and the core of it survives. Averaged over 4 seeds with fixed trees, C2 gains +0.00120 (2023) and +0.00075 (2024), and every placebo stays between about -0.0005 and +0.0002. The subsidence pattern behind it holds in the raw data in every year: claims on clay with a dry summer index of 0.7 or more run at about 6 times the rate elsewhere, the production model under-predicts that cell (A/E 1.17 and 1.36 against 1.04), and C2 closes part of the gap. On 2022, which the finder never scanned, the gain is positive (+0.0007 / +0.0004) while the random placebo is null.
The refutation does succeed against half of the candidate. x_fz3_rain has no physical support: flood frequency does not vary with rainfall within any flood zone. It adds about zero shape and moves the 2024 level by 1.2%. The test should therefore centre on x_clay_dry alone, which gives +0.00059 / +0.00083 with no change in level.
Caveats: the finder's single-seed headline (+0.00095 / +0.00188) overstates the effect. One seed of four gives only +0.00018 on 2024. Each year's bootstrap interval only just reaches or includes zero. The gain sits entirely in claims above 20k. The 2025 total moves by -0.9% to 0%, which interacts with #143.
It is worth testing because the mechanism is real and measurable in the raw data and the gain clears every placebo. The owner should seed-average the comparison and apply D-23 before adopting it.

title: Buildings: one-parameter calibration power (slope on log rate) for the under-dispersed small-claim XGBoost, estimated out of time
gain_2023: +0.00045 (small-part form, small x (r/gm)^(b-1) with b = 1.093 fitted on 2024, sum of the small part kept, large part unchanged; customer bootstrap 95% -0.00029 to +0.00122). Total form with a = 1.095 from 2024: +0.00037. Measured on the no-CANN backtest predictions; not a refit.
gain_2024: +0.00056 (small-part form, b = 1.074 fitted on 2023; 95% +0.00004 to +0.00111). Total form with a = 1.078 from 2023: +0.00055. Joint customer bootstrap of the two-year mean, with customers shared across the years: +0.00051 (95% +0.00005 to +0.00097), P(gain <= 0) = 1.5%.
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. AUDIT_LOG A20 only says that isotonic recalibration "failed the two-year rule in scratch probes", with no numbers, no form and no line given. The D-21 level factor and the tilt change only the level. Nothing in python/ or config.json changes the slope of the buildings prediction. A one-parameter monotone stretch is materially new.

(2) Signal, re-measured with my own scripts and the probe. Baseline D2 reproduces exactly (0.11102 / 0.11046), and the decomposition file matches mu to 6e-9.
- Every form clears +0.0003 on both years except one: the total form with a fitted at a free level gives a = 1.101/1.137, which lands only +0.00016 on 2023. Fitting with the sum kept reproduces the finder's a of 1.078/1.095.
- A fixed exponent from 1.02 to 1.15 (small-part form) is positive on both years. From 1.05 to 1.10 it gives +0.00033 to +0.00065.
- Uncertainty in b: I refitted b on 60 customer resamples of the fitting year. b ranged 1.02 to 1.15, and the gain on the other year was positive in all 60 (5-95%: 2023 +0.00027 to +0.00045, 2024 +0.00018 to +0.00068).
- The probe on mu deciles gives +0.00037 / +0.00049, which matches the finder. After the stretch it gives -0.00030 / -0.00046, so the stretch absorbs that pattern.
- Which part carries the gain: the stretch on the tree rate gives +0.00043 / +0.00051. Stretching only the credibility factor gives +0.00003 / +0.00005.

(3) Large claims. This refutes the finder's own explanation: the gain is not driven by large claims.
- Dropping the top 1, 3, 5, 10 or 20 claim rows leaves +0.00043 to +0.00053 on both years.
- Capping row y at 50k, 100k or 250k gives +0.00071 / +0.00068, +0.00055 / +0.00056 and +0.00046 / +0.00053.
- Excluding every row with a claim over 50k gives about +0.0010 on both years.
- Rows over 50k contribute negatively (-0.00040 / -0.00025). The gain comes from lowering the lowest-rate decile and raising the highest.
- The 'disappears at 50k' result does reproduce in one setting: scoring the small part alone against y_small with its sum kept (-0.00009 / +0.00012). That is a level artefact. The stretch lowers the deviance-optimal level by about 1.5% (k rises from 1.020 to 1.037 and from 1.046 to 1.059). At each model's own optimal level, the small-target gain is +0.00026 / +0.00040.

(4) Structural cause, found rather than assumed. The in-sample optimal exponent is about 1.20 (1.215 for the 2021-22 fit, 1.195 for 2021-23). So the booster is under-fitted even in sample, which is consistent with heavy regularisation: a minimum leaf hessian of 20,000, eta 0.05 and 131 early-stopped trees. The GLM lines do not show it: contents a = 0.91/0.98 fails, and motor a = 1.06/1.04 gives +0.00016/+0.00003, which is noise.

(5) Risks.
- The level-reset form (deviance level kept in sample) raises the level by 1.9-2.0% on the backtest years. It scores +0.00061 / +0.00082, and the extra over the sum-kept form is a level bet that rides on #143.
- Keeping the sum costs only about 0.00003 if the level is already right.
- b comes from the selection years, and the 2023 leg uses 2024 data. The fixed-grid and resampling results make the exact b unimportant, but the effect itself was found on these years.
- My predictions exclude CANN. CANN is trained in sample, where the optimum is about 1.2, so it may already absorb part of the stretch.
- Pooled across the three Kaggle lines, buildings is 31-34% of the null deviance, so +0.0005 on buildings is about +0.00015 to +0.0002 pooled.
recommended_test:
Pre-register a single form before running anything.

The change, in python/run_glm_lines.py, buildings only, behind a new config.json switch such as glm_lines.power_calibration.buildings:
- After the small-claim prediction, including CANN since CANN applies within the model's predict, set small' = small x (r/gm(r))^(b-1), where r = small/exposure and gm is the geometric mean over the rows being predicted.
- Rescale small' so the rows' small-part sum is unchanged.
- Leave the large-claim term and the credibility factor untouched. Apply rebalancing and the tilt as now.
- Estimate b on out-of-time predictions only, minimising Tweedie p = 1.5 deviance of k x stretched small against the per-claim-capped small target (y_small) with a free level k.
- For the 2024 leg, use b from the 2023 leg's predictions (no CANN: 1.074).
- For the 2023 leg, preferably add a nested window ([2021], 2022) in a scratch copy of the harness and take b from it. Only if that is impossible, use the 2024 leg's b (1.093) and flag it as look-ahead.
- For 2025, use the mean of the two out-of-time values (about 1.08).
- Re-estimate b on the CANN-included predictions, because CANN may overlap.

How to run it: use the gap_tests.py / combined_tests.py pattern. window_preds over rgl.EVAL_WINDOWS with baseline_build, buildings trees held at the baseline 131, and compare() with the paired 1,000-resample customer bootstrap (ev_g8 style). Apply the two-year rule and the D-23 significance rule for discretionary additions, with the joint two-year interval.
- Report the deviance-level-preserving variant (about +2% level) only as a sensitivity. Do not adopt it unless the buildings level (#143) is argued separately under D-21.
- Run it jointly with C11 (more trees or smaller leaves), not stacked on it.
- The owner should run this, because these harnesses append to the audit log.
reasoning:
My own measurement clears the bar on both years: +0.00045 / +0.00056 in the pre-registrable form, against a noise floor of about +0.0003. The joint customer bootstrap puts the two-year mean at +0.00051, with a 95% interval of +0.00005 to +0.00097.

It is robust:
- to the exact exponent (positive anywhere from 1.02 to 1.15);
- to estimation error in that exponent (all 60 resamples gain);
- to the choice of form (total, small part, y_small or y_full);
- to removing large claims: if anything the gain grows without them.

There is also a structural reason I measured myself. The buildings XGBoost is under-dispersed even in sample (optimal exponent about 1.2), which matches its heavy regularisation, and the GLM lines show no such effect.

Two of the finder's claims are wrong:
- The gain does not come from large claims landing in the highest-ranked rows. It is attritional, and large-claim rows count against it.
- The level-reset variant's extra gain is a roughly 2% level bet on the known buildings under-prediction (#143), not shape, so it should not be bundled in.

Three things keep this at 'worth testing' rather than 'adopt':
- The effect was found and its exponent set on the selection years. A nested 2021 to 2022 leg would settle that.
- These backtest predictions exclude CANN, which may absorb part of the stretch.
- The pooled leaderboard effect is small, about +0.0002.

title: Motor own-line credibility: tune k on the small-claim (or capped) target, giving k=3-4 instead of 8 (k=6 if the literal rule is kept)
gain_2023: My own measurement: I rebuilt the production motor model exactly, and it matches backtest_preds_motor mu to a relative difference of 0 in both years (D2 0.10097 in 2023, 0.08062 in 2024). Gains are against k=8. Full developed target: k=4 -0.00017 (bootstrap 95% -0.00185 to +0.00114); k=6 +0.000035 (-0.00055 to +0.00049); k=3 -0.00066. On robust bases k=4 gains: without the single 15.25m row +0.00072 (+0.00078 to +0.00083 when the top 3 or top 10 rows are dropped); capped at 1m +0.00066 (95% +0.00015 to +0.00118, significant); capped at 250k +0.00074; capped at 100k +0.00073; small-claim part against the small-claim target +0.00063. Matching the level changes nothing (-0.00019 against -0.00017 on the full target). The 15.25m row alone contributes -0.00084 to the k=4 v k=8 difference. Pooled over the three lines: k=4 -0.00008, k=6 +0.00002.
gain_2024: Gains against k=8. Full developed target: k=4 +0.00131 (95% +0.00035 to +0.00249; probability of not being better 0.004); k=6 +0.00057 (+0.00023 to +0.00099); k=3 +0.00164. Robust bases for k=4: without the top row +0.00092 (the 1.32m row favours k=4 by +0.00040); without the top 10 rows +0.00070; capped at 1m +0.00122 (+0.00034 to +0.00226); capped at 100k +0.00087; small-claim part +0.00072; against the reported target +0.00112; level-matched +0.00133. Pooled over the three lines: k=4 +0.00059, k=6 +0.00026. Two-year mean intervals (pack formula): k=4 full +0.00057 (-0.00035 to +0.00149, not significant); k=6 full +0.00030 (-0.00002 to +0.00063, borderline); k=4 capped at 1m +0.00094 (+0.00040 to +0.00148, significant).
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. k was tuned once, in A16, on 2023 only against the uncapped developed target, over the grid 0.5/1/2/4/8/16/32/64/inf (config glm_lines.credibility_k_grid; run_glm_lines.run_line lines 290-300). I grepped AUDIT_LOG, DECISIONS, MODEL_DOCUMENTATION and python/. There is no later re-tune, and nothing in 5.3 or A17-A26 covers it, so the candidate is new.

(2) Signal. I did not use the finder's numbers. I rebuilt motor myself with extract.py: the pack's prepare() run in memory with no out_dir, so no evidence, no run log and no bytecode written. This reproduces ev_g2 exactly (k=8 0.096840) and the backtest mu exactly. The original grid never tried 6. With a finer grid, the pack's own literal 2023 rule picks k=6 (0.096859 against 0.096840), with no sight of 2024.

On 2023 alone, three robust tuning criteria each pick k=4 independently: small-claim part against the small-claim target, y capped at 1m, and the 15.25m row excluded. Applied out of sample to 2024, k=4 gives +0.00131, which is significant.

The 2023 full-target loss comes from one row: a developed 15.25m bodily-injury claim (reported/developed 0.78) on a customer with no prior own-line claims. That row contributes -0.00084. Dropping the top 1, 3 or 10 rows leaves k=4 at +0.0007 to +0.0008 in 2023 and +0.0007 to +0.0012 in 2024, so neither year rests on a single claim once that row is handled.

Level-matched gains are almost identical to the raw gains, so the effect is discrimination, not level. title: Buildings: part-year rows cost less than pro rata; add an exposure elasticity to the large-claim GLM (or a short-row factor)
gain_2023: Short-row factor 0.4 on rows with exposure <= 0.1 (rebalanced): +0.00048. Factor estimated on 2024 and applied to 2023 (f* = 0.40): +0.00047. Elasticity b = 1.10: +0.00053, but only +0.00027 once rows <= 0.1 are left out. Six exposure bands, scaled relative to full-year rows and fitted on 2024 (k = 20): +0.00093. Pure level change of x1.0015: +0.00001, so the gain is not a rebalancing artefact.
gain_2024: Short-row factor 0.4: +0.00070. Factor estimated on 2023 (f* = 0.48): +0.00067. Elasticity b = 1.10: +0.00054, but only +0.00012 once rows <= 0.1 are left out (fails the +0.0003 bar). Six bands fitted on 2023 (k = 20): +0.00086. Customer bootstrap of the two-year mean (1,000 draws): factor 0.4 +0.00059 (-0.00010 to +0.00120); factor fitted on the other year +0.00057 (-0.00003 to +0.00107); six bands k = 20 +0.00094 (+0.00007 to +0.00177); eight bands k = 200 +0.00064 (+0.00002 to +0.00118).
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. I searched AUDIT_LOG, MODEL_DOCUMENTATION, DECISIONS, config.json, python/ and sql/ for any short-row factor, part-year term, exposure elasticity or exposure as a covariate. There is none. Exposure appears only as an offset; A21/D-22 seasonal exposure is a different mechanism. Bridget's branch used exposure as an XGBoost feature, but that was never tested on this model. I also combined A21-style seasonal weights (by frequency, capped cost or total cost, fitted on the fitting years) with the short-row factor. Seasonality alone is still -0.0003 to -0.0007 on both years, and adding it to the short-row factor lowers the factor's gain. So seasonality does not explain the effect.

(2) Signal. I reproduced the finder's numbers exactly. Raw data for all four years, not just the backtest: buildings rows <= 36 days have normal claim frequency (0.050 against 0.044), but their mean claim size, capped at 50k, is 3.3k against 7.7k. This holds in every year (1.1k / 3.5k / 3.3k / 4.6k against 6.7k to 7.5k for the same winter months on longer rows). Every peril is lower within itself (escape of water 3.7k against 5.7k; storm 2.8k against 3.5k; the 5 fire, flood and subsidence claims are all under 5k). The 90th percentile is 6.7k against 21k, and the largest claim is 17.9k across 64 claims. A peril-stratified permutation test gives one-sided p = 0.0001. Claim size falls steadily as rows get shorter (<= 0.05: 2.9k; 0.05-0.1: 3.5k; 0.1-0.15: 5.4k; 0.15-0.2: 6.7k; over 0.5: 7.9k). On full-year rows, claims in the first or last 36 days are not small (6.8k to 7.3k), so the effect belongs to short rows, not to time within a row.

Not a leak: renewal_decision is absent from the test file, and the short-row flag comes only from the period dates. Test has 7,357 rows <= 0.1, the same mix as 2022-24. The effect also appears in 2021-23, which are fully developed, so it is not a development artefact. Claims match to rows by policy and loss date, rows never overlap, and there is no sign the matching creates the effect.

No large claim drives it: there are no claims over 50k on short rows in any year. Most of the gain comes from lower predictions on about 7,400 claim-free short rows (+0.0015 a year), partly offset by the 15 to 17 claim rows (-0.0008 to -0.0011).

(3) Refuting the finder's mechanism. The candidate says the shortfall is in large claims. My measurement says otherwise. With the target capped at 50k (prediction scaled pro rata), short rows still sit at 0.42 / 0.55 of the rest, and the factor still gains +0.00017 to +0.00041. Capped at 10k they sit at 0.68 / 0.87. So most of the missing cost is in claims of 10k to 50k, which belong to the XGBoost small-claim model. Per short row, the expected excess over 50k is about 29k a year, against a shortfall of about 69k below 50k. A log-exposure term in the excess GLM alone could therefore recover only about 30% of the effect. Across bands, large-claim frequency per 1,000 exposure is 0 / 1.1 / 1.3 / 1.7 / 1.9 / 1.6. It does not rise steadily with exposure, so b > 1 for large claims is not supported. The finder's 'capped -0.00004' result probably came from scoring capped y against the uncapped prediction. I also could not reproduce the claim that 'excluding declined_by_insurer rows makes b = 1.1 negative': scoring only those rows gives +0.0012 / +0.0007. That subset is unreliable anyway (A/E about 0.5, and the label is outcome-driven and absent from test).

(4) Risk. The bootstrap interval for the single short-row factor includes zero narrowly, so it would probably fail the D-23 significance test on this proxy. The payoff is also lopsided. One extra 20k claim on a typical short row wipes out a year's gain (-0.0005), and one 100k claim costs -0.0025. If the effect were not real, the expected loss would be about -0.0011 a year. The threshold of 0.1 was chosen after seeing both years. Contents and motor show no short-row shortfall in claim size (contents 3.3k against 2.8k; motor 3.5k against 3.5k). This is buildings only, the cause in the generator is unknown, and the rows carry only about 0.25% of predicted cost.

Drop the excess-GLM elasticity, which targets the wrong component, and test a post-model short-row factor on the total buildings prediction (small-claim XGBoost + excess + CANN). Pre-register it before running.

Primary: buildings rows with exposure_plain <= 0.1 (36 days or fewer) get factor f_w. For each window, f_w = deviance-optimal scale for those rows relative to the other rows, computed from the window's own in-sample fitted predictions on its fitting years only (2021-22 for score 2023; 2021-23 for score 2024). Apply no shrinkage, or a light k of about 20 claims. Then rebalance so the line total is unchanged. For 2025, estimate f from 2021-24 in-sample.

Secondary, pre-registered as a sensitivity: six bands (<= 0.1, <= 0.25, <= 0.5, <= 0.75, < 1, full), scaled relative to full-year rows and estimated the same way. It gained +0.0009 on both years and its two-year mean was significant in my proxy. Report thresholds 0.1 and 0.15 as well, without choosing between them on the score years.

Implementation: a scratch harness in the gap_tests.py / combined_tests.py style. Reuse combined_tests.baseline_build and window_preds. Add the fitting-year in-sample predictions, which window_preds does not return now. Apply the factor in a new variant function. Score under the two-year rule against the production model, then the paired customer-cluster bootstrap (A20) for the D-23 two-year-mean significance test. Write any new evidence under audit/evidence/glm_lines/ only once the owner approves a logged run.

Check before adopting: confirm the in-sample short-row A/E in each fitting year (expect about 0.2 to 0.6). If f_w estimated in-sample comes out near 1, stop.
reasoning:
The finder's raw measurements reproduce exactly. A short-row factor clears +0.0003 on both years (+0.00048 / +0.00070), including when the factor is estimated on the other year (+0.00047 / +0.00067). It is not a leak and not one large claim, and it is new: the pack uses exposure only as an offset. There is also a structural signal rather than a lucky band. Short buildings rows have about half the normal claim size in every year 2021-24. The shortfall holds within every peril (peril-stratified p of about 0.0001) and grows steadily as rows get shorter, while frequency is normal. Seasonality does not explain it, and combining the factor with seasonal exposure does not help.

The candidate as written needs correcting. Its preferred form (log exposure in the buildings excess GLM, or exposure^b) targets the wrong component: most of the shortfall is in claims of 10k to 50k inside the XGBoost small-claim model. Outside the <= 0.1 rows, the elasticity's gain falls to +0.00027 / +0.00012. So the testable form is a factor on the total prediction for rows <= 0.1, or a banded relativity by exposure, estimated on each window's fitting years.

The case against is real. The two-year-mean bootstrap interval for the single factor narrowly includes zero, so it may fail D-23. The payoff is lopsided: one extra 20k to 100k claim on a short row costs more than a year's gain. The threshold was chosen after seeing both years, the effect is buildings-only with no known cause in the generator, and the prize is small. It is about +0.0005 to +0.0007 on buildings D2, and less on a pooled Kaggle D2 by buildings' share of the null deviance, which I did not measure.

It is cheap, the downside is bounded, and the evidence is strong and consistent, so it is worth one pre-registered run. Expectations should be set: the six-band version is the likelier to pass D-23, and the single flag may pass the two-year rule but fail significance.

Among recent losses, the closed share falls from 93% (July 2024) to 18.5% (December 2024), yet incidence among the closed stays at 28-32%. December 2024 losses already closed (n=128) recover at 30.5%, the same as fully settled years.
- Open case estimates are gross. Q4 2024 open average is 2,790, against a closed gross average of 2,636 (a closed net average would be about 2,000).
- My re-implementation of the product-limit development matches ev_10_development.csv to the unit for both perils.
- Expected missing recovery: 1.343m reported and 1.461m developed for 2024, about 1.24% of developed motor and 1.38% of the small-claim pool (claims capped at 50k). Policy year 2023 is 0.007m. The amount-weighted rates are stable whichever loss years estimate them: 0.232/0.234/0.236 for own damage and 0.040/0.039/0.040 for theft, using loss years to 2022, 2023 and 2024.

(3) Leak or single-claim effect? Not a leak: the deduction uses claim status and incurred at the valuation date, exactly as the target already does, and changes only the target. It is spread over 2,189 rows, not one large claim.

(4) Risks.
- The two-year rule cannot see it. Its training years are mature in both backtests, so the bias exists only in production. Applied mechanically, the rule would reject it (2023 +0.0000, 2024 -0.0003 from the basis change alone).
- The score effect is level-only and small. A 1.2% level bias near the optimum costs about 0.00002 D2 per year. Relative to doing nothing, the gain is about +0.0001 if motor is about 4% high (2024 k on the adjusted target) and about +0.0003 if it is 7-9% high, as C1 suggests. If motor is otherwise slightly low, the gain is negative but bounded at about -0.0001.
- The 2023 k of 1.022 rests on the single 11.9m claim: without that one row k is 0.92, though dropping the largest row always lowers k, so this is not proof that motor is high.
- If Kaggle's truth were a later snapshot rather than true ultimate, the correction would be wrong. The overview states ultimate net of recoveries twice.
- Double counting: if C1 or #151 sets a motor level factor from the 2024 backtest, it must be measured on the same (adjusted) target.
reasoning:
On a D2 measurement this fails the bar. 2023 gains nothing, and the 2024 change is a target-basis effect, so the score cannot be compared. As a level effect it is about -0.0001/+0.0001, well under +0.0003 on both years. I still rate it worth testing because the structural reason is strong.
- The competition defines the target as ultimate cost net of recoveries.
- The data show a mechanical recovery rule: ratios of exactly 0.8 and 0.3, and incidence independent of year, size, lag and how fast a claim settles. Recoveries are booked only at closure.
- The production fit therefore overstates its most recent year (2024) by about 1.25% of motor, or 1.4% of the small-claim pool. That year carries a weight of 1.0 in the log-linear projection to 2025.
- No backtest saw this bias, because their training years were mature (0.007m affected). It is a production-only bias, not something the two-year rule has already validated.

The fix is cheap, deterministic and testable as a data fix. Its D2 downside is bounded at about -0.0001, and its expected sign is positive given every motor level diagnostic: the 2024 k on the adjusted target is 0.961, development backtests overshoot motor by x1.035 and x1.055, and the level in #151 looks high. The expected score gain is low, roughly +0.00002 to +0.0003 motor D2 and less once pooled across lines. It should be presented as a correctness fix, not a score improvement.

title: Count-weighted (or 100k-capped) reporting pattern for motor bodily injury
gain_2023: The target basis changes, so D2 cannot be compared directly. As a proxy I applied the change's level effect to the motor backtest predictions (mu x0.988): motor D2 moves by -0.00010 and pooled D2 by -0.00005. The development backtest as at 2022-12-31 gives BI developed/actual 1.0866 (cost) against 1.0539 (count) and motor 1.0346 against 1.0210, measured against the cost yardstick. With a consistent count yardstick the figures are BI 1.0593 and motor 1.0231.
gain_2024: Same proxy: motor D2 moves by +0.00008 and pooled D2 by +0.00004. That is the opposite sign to 2023 and about a tenth of the noise threshold. Even the best possible rescale for each year gains only about 0.0001. The development backtest as at 2023-12-31 gives BI 1.1339 (cost) against 1.0841 (count) and motor 1.0546 against 1.0335. With a consistent yardstick the figures are BI 1.0948 and motor 1.0378.
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. The idea is new. sql/10 computes f_cnt only for the evidence column n_ibnr_count_basis. A15 validated only the cost pattern. A25 tested recent weighting (pattern_decay), not size weighting. Nothing in AUDIT_LOG, DECISIONS, config.json or python/ tests count against cost.

(2) Signal. I wrote a read-only replica of backtest_development.py. It uses an in-memory DuckDB, swaps the pattern weight by string substitution, and writes nothing to the pack. The cost basis reproduces ev_d2 exactly, and every figure the finder gave (cost, 1m cap, 100k cap, count) reproduces exactly against the cost yardstick. The direction also survives three harder yardsticks:
- the count pattern on both sides;
- the D-11 lift on both sides (BI 1.0445 cost against 1.0196 count as at 2022; 1.0673 against 1.0346 as at 2023);
- the D-11 lift plus 2-6% a year inflation (at 6%, BI 1.0166 cost against 0.9932 count as at 2022; 1.0341 against 1.0046 as at 2023).

The candidate's premise, however, is contradicted by the data, and the yardstick is biased in a way that favours count:
(a) Size and lag are not independent. I looked at the fully observed window: BI losses 2021-22 with lag up to 730 days. Claims reported after 366-730 days have a mean incurred of 25.6k, against 20.3-22.7k at shorter lags. Their cost share is 14.7% against a count share of 12.5%, even though 33% are open against 13%. For 2022 losses the median is 16% higher and the mean capped at 100k is 14% higher; for 2021 the excess sits only in the tail. Mean lag rises with size band (168 to 178 days), and the share reported after 365 days rises from 11.5% to 14%. Cost weighting captures a real effect.
(b) The yardstick is least mature for exactly the claims at issue. At current incurred, the mean size of late-reported BI claims relative to early-reported ones falls with recency:
- 2021: 1.064 (21% open, paid/incurred 0.86);
- 2022: 1.030 (37% open, 0.75);
- 2023: about 0.96 excluding the 11.89m claim (66% open, 0.50).
So a method that assumes late claims are the size of early ones scores well against current incurred for the wrong reason. A uniform IBNER lift does not remove this differential. The two backtest points share this bias and part of their data.
(c) Concentration. As at 2023, the single 11.89m claim accounts for about 58% of the cost-to-count gap: capping it at 1m alone takes BI from 1.134 to 1.105. As at 2022, about 70% of the gap comes from the roughly 95 claims between 100k and 1m, which is tail noise.

(3) Risk. The change lowers the target basis, with BI 2024 down 3.2% and motor 2024/2023/2022 down 1.25%/0.46%/0.22% in my production-valuation rerun, so the two-year rule cannot judge it. The 2025 effect is a motor level cut of about 1.0-1.4%, whose D2 value depends on the unknown 2025 truth, and the proxy is below noise with opposite signs. Four weighting variants were tried and the best was picked on the same two backtest points. It is not a leak.
recommended_test: None recommended. If the owner still wants to revisit it as part of C1, the cleanest check is to edit sql/10 in a copy: in the wc CTE add pw = CASE WHEN line='motor' AND peril='bodily_injury' THEN 1.0 ELSE net_cost END, then use w*pw in place of w*net_cost in both events rows. Re-run the development backtest from a copy of the backtest logic, not the logging runner. My read-only replica is <review scratch>/agents/verify-C13/replica.py. Run it with the pack's .venv python and PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1; its outputs are replica_out.csv and replica_prod.csv in the same folder. Any adoption should also pass a size-lag check on a more mature yardstick, for example closed claims only, or paid to date by lag. Note too that the motor level question in #151 (16% above the best leaderboard file) dwarfs this change's effect of about 1.2%; that should be settled as an explicit level decision, not by changing the development method.
reasoning: I reproduced the finder's development-backtest numbers exactly. Count weighting does bring BI and motor developed/actual closer to 1 at both valuation dates, and this holds under every yardstick variant I tried, including IBNER with inflation. However, the stated premise that BI lag does not depend on size is false in the fully observed window: late-reported claims are about 14-22% larger. And the yardstick's late-reported claims are systematically immature: they are the most open, and their size relative to early claims falls from 1.06 to 0.96 as loss years get more recent. That is exactly the bias that would make a lower-IBNR method look better. Over half the as-at-2023 gain is one claim; most of the as-at-2022 gain is about 95 tail claims. On the score side, the change is a level-only cut of about 1.2% to 2025 motor. On the backtest predictions that moves motor D2 by -0.0001 in 2023 and +0.00008 in 2024 (pooled about ±0.00005), opposite signs and well below the 0.0003 noise threshold. A change in development basis also makes D2 incomparable. There is no strong structural case, the measurable gain is negligible, and there is a plausible reason the backtest flatters it. Hence not worth testing.

Buildings: -0.0001 (production mu basis, CI [-0.0005, +0.0004]).
gain_2024: Motor, proxy vintage as at 2023-12-31 (fit 2021-23, score 2024). (2) Mechanism: confirmed, and sharper than claimed. My own in-memory reproduction of sql/10 matches production y_full exactly (max abs diff 0 on both lines; bf 1.8816 and 1.4289). Developed 2024 motor BI by quarter is 18.5/12.9/10.6/3.9m under yearly BF and 12.0/10.3/12.1/11.6m under quarterly allocation; the Q4 factor goes to 5.64 (x1.163 IBNER). Development backtest, RMS log error by quarter, yearly against quarterly: as at 2022-12-31, BI 0.44 vs 0.09 and subsidence 0.40 vs 0.11; as at 2023-12-31, BI 0.44 vs 0.19 and subsidence 0.37 vs 0.07. The 2024 diagnostics are distorted: motor exit-row k is 1.14 (0.88 in 2023), and rows whose midpoint falls in Q1 have k 1.68 (0.80 in 2023). On the quarterly basis these become 1.01 and 1.32. Production 2024 motor D2 is 0.0806 against the yearly-basis actual and 0.0877 against the quarterly one (a basis change, not a gain).

(3) Score: the motor GLM has no timing feature (no new_business, start month or row type). In the final 2021-24 fit, quarterly BF changes the 4-year one-way totals of the model's features by an exposure-weighted RMS of only 0.2-1.4%, with alternating signs, for example across NCB years. That is reshuffled noise, not signal. At the same time the change concentrates 2024 Q4 BI IBNR on 120 reported claims grossed up x6.55, against 1,178 claims at x2.19 now, which adds target variance. In feature-level bias as at 2022-12-31, quarterly BF is worse than yearly on channel, payment, credit, segment, region and NCB. As at 2023-12-31 it looks better, but only because yearly BF multiplies the 11.9m Q2 claim by 1.71.

Proxy refits (Tweedie GLM on the production motor features, split at 50k on reported cost as in glm_lines.split_targets, two penalty/band specs) give no gain above +0.0003 on both years. The 2023 gain disappears once the 11.9m row is excluded, all 2024 results are at or below zero, and every bootstrap CI includes zero. Buildings (subsidence, 1.4m reallocated) is noise in both directions. Caveat: the proxy is not the production model (no splines, no credibility history, no GPD scaling, no XGBoost for buildings), and the vintages give the BF year 1/2 and 1/3 of the training weight, against 1/4 in the final fit. recommended_test: Not recommended as a score change. If the team wants it for reporting hygiene only (cleaner 2024 motor diagnostics by row type and month; it does not change the level or #151), the change is in sql/10_development.sql after bf_year. Build a bfq table per line x peril x ay x loss quarter: rep_q, f_q from ibnr_factor_by_quarter, exposure days in the quarter, ult_q_raw = rep_q + (1 - 1/f_q) x prior_rate x expo_q, rescaled so the sum over quarters equals reported x bf_factor. In line_claims_dev, use ult_q / rep_q in place of b.bf_factor. The only valid score test is a vintage one with run_glm_lines-equivalent fits, since the pack's backtests never put BF into training data (valuation 2024-12-31 throughout). My scripts in <review scratch>/agents/verify-C14/ (dev.py, vintage.py, transplant.py) do this with a proxy GLM. Any such test must report results with the 11.9m 2023 BI row excluded. A materially different variant, if anything is tried, is to allocate the BF unreported amount to exposure (a reported-claims fit with a row-level quarterly-BF reporting offset) rather than grossing up the few Q4 reported claims x6.5. Note that the related offset test (A25/dv1) was neutral.
reasoning: The candidate's diagnosis is right: a single BF factor per loss year over-develops Q1 and under-develops Q4. By quarter it is clearly the worse reserve allocation (RMS log error about 0.4 against 0.1-0.2 in both development backtests), and it distorts the 2024 motor backtest actual by row type and month. But the score depends on whether the timing bias reaches the model's features, and for motor it barely does. The GLM has no exposure-timing feature, and the one-way effect on its features in the final fit is 0.2-1.4% of noise-like reshuffling. In exchange, quarterly allocation puts about 11.6m of 2024 BI on 120 Q4 claims at x6.55, which raises target variance. My vintage proxy refits give motor 2023 gains that come entirely from the single 11.9m claim (negative once it is excluded) and motor 2024 changes of -0.0004 to 0, all within bootstrap noise. Buildings is noise in both directions. The level is unchanged by construction, so it does nothing for #151. The variant measured here is the candidate's, and it does not clear the +0.0003-on-both-years bar. The one benefit is cleaner 2024 diagnostics, which is a reporting point, not a scoring gain.

title: Region R11 elevation is recorded in feet, not metres: divide by 3.28084 before any model sees it
gain_2023: My own in-memory refit, without CANN, trees fixed at 131, history E recomputed. Buildings: a mean of -0.00009 over 6 XGBoost seeds (20261021, 11-15), with a same-seed SD of 0.00047. Only 2 of the 6 seeds were positive, and the production seed gave -0.00013. Customer-cluster bootstrap 95% CI: -0.00125 to +0.00116. R11 rows contribute +0.00011 and the other rows -0.00020. The deterministic GLM parts alone (excess plus frequency GLM, XGBoost left on raw elevation) give -0.00009 to -0.00011. Contents: +0.00031 (bootstrap -0.00020 to +0.00087). Probe-style check restricted to R11 bands of corrected elevation (fit 2024, score 2023, k=200): buildings +0.00015 to +0.00039; contents -0.00020 to +0.00015.
gain_2024: Buildings: a mean of +0.00078 over 6 seeds, SD 0.00023, with all 6 seeds positive (+0.00047 to +0.00105). The production seed gave +0.00061. Bootstrap 95% CI: -0.00028 to +0.00190. R11 rows contribute +0.00110 and the other rows -0.00032. The GLM parts alone give -0.00005. Contents: +0.00017, but R11 rows give -0.00001 and the other rows +0.00018, so the contents gain does not come through the R11 mechanism. Probe restricted to R11 (fit 2023, score 2024, k=200): buildings +0.00020 to +0.00058; contents -0.00026 to +0.00015. Out of window (fit 2023-24, score 2022, no credibility): buildings +0.00023, 3 of 3 seeds positive.
refutation_attempted:
(1) Novelty. Searched docs/MODEL_DOCUMENTATION.md, audit/AUDIT_LOG.md, audit/DECISIONS.md, config.json, python/ and sql/ for R11, feet, 3.28 and elevation. Nothing treats R11 elevation as a unit error. Elevation enters as raw values or splines (A17, D-18) and as f_elev_band in sql/08. The idea is new.

(2) Is the data error real? I re-queried addresses myself. R11 runs at 3.25 to 3.30 times the other regions at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles (5.6/24.6/67.6 against 1.7/7.5/20.7). The other 11 regions cap at exactly 60.0 (197 rows sit at the cap). R11 reaches 196.9, which is 60 x 3.28084, with 20 rows above 196, and 13.5% of R11 lies at or above 60 against 0.04% elsewhere. Within each flood zone, R11's median is 3.25 to 3.29 times the others'. R11's distance to river (3.13 km) and flood zone mean (1.51) match the other regions, so R11 is not genuinely hillier terrain. Its values sit on a 0.1 grid, consistent with converting to feet and then rounding. I regard the unit error as established.

(3) Signal. I did not reuse the critic's scripts. I wrote my own refit, verify-G1/refit_g1.py. It differs from the critic's in four ways: it also re-bands the contents f_elev_band used by the frequency GLM behind E (my reproduction of the SQL banding matched 100%), it uses different seeds, it splits the GLM parts from the XGBoost, and it adds a buildings 2022 out-of-window check. The baseline reproduces the critic's figures exactly (contents 0.09538 / 0.09677; buildings seed 20261021 0.11102 / 0.11046). Re-banding f_elev_band changes nothing to 5 decimal places.

The production backtest predictions show a monotone A/E gradient within R11 by corrected elevation in both years for buildings. In 2023 A/E runs from 1.86 under 1 m to about 0.70-0.74 above 15 m; in 2024 from 1.34-2.6 on low ground to about 0.55-0.68 on high ground. The R11-only cross-year probe confirms this signal on both years for buildings, but not for contents.

(4) Leak and concentration checks. It is not a leak: elevation is a static address attribute. It is not driven by large claims: excluding the 10 largest claims raises the 2024 buildings gain to +0.0012. The gain does sit in a few rows, though: the 10 rows with the largest change in deviance give +0.00106 against a net +0.00078. These are R11 claims on low ground, which fits the mechanism. The largest single row is +0.00016.

(5) Risk. There is no change to the target basis, so D2 stays comparable. Selection risk is low, because the issue was found from distributions, not from scores. My band choices in the R11 probe were made after seeing the A/E table, but all settings at the default k=200 are positive on both years.

Against the candidate:
- Buildings 2023 is nil or negative on the refit, so the change fails the pack's strict two-year rule. A true gain of about +0.0002 to +0.0003 is still consistent with the noise (SE about 0.00019).
- The deterministic GLM parts are slightly negative on both years (-0.00005 to -0.00011).
- The contents gain is a side effect of the spline's top knot moving from 197 to 60, not the R11 fix itself. The critic's out-of-window contents results are mixed (-0.00015, -0.00031, +0.00045), so contents should be treated as zero.
recommended_test:
Treat it as a data correction behind a decision switch, like D-02, D-09 and D-24.

1. In config.json, add a decisions entry with sql_variable d26_r11_elevation_feet, apply true.
2. In sql/03_build_contents.sql (contents_model join) and in sql/11_line_models.sql (buildings_model and motor_model joins), change `ad.* EXCLUDE (address_id)` to `ad.* EXCLUDE (address_id) REPLACE (CASE WHEN getvariable('d26_r11_elevation_feet') AND ad.region = 'R11' THEN round(ad.elevation_m / 3.28084, 2) ELSE ad.elevation_m END AS elevation_m)`. Keep the raw value as elevation_m_raw if wanted. Because sql/08 bands contents_model, the f_elev_band boundaries and the test rows then follow automatically.
3. Before switching it on, measure in memory with the gap_tests harness pattern (rgl.prepare, then edit line.df, then rgl.expected_history for every window, then build and predict per EVAL window). Use at least 6 XGBoost seeds with trees fixed at the baseline's tuned count, plus the customer-cluster bootstrap and the 2022 out-of-window check.
4. A ready harness is <review scratch>/agents/verify-G1/refit_g1.py. Summarise with summ_g1.py in the same folder; results are in results_g1.csv. Run it with `.venv/bin/python -B` from the pack root.
5. Success check: the R11 buildings A/E by corrected elevation band flattens towards 1.

Expect a buildings two-year mean of about +0.0003 (2024 about +0.0008, 2023 about 0) and about 0 on contents, so roughly +0.0001 pooled. Adopting it would need the owner to accept it as a correctness fix (the D-24 precedent), because it does not pass the strict two-year rule on buildings 2023.
reasoning:
The data error is real and not documented anywhere in the pack. R11 elevation is in feet: a constant 3.28x ratio at every quantile and within every flood zone, the 60 m cap appearing as 196.9, and identical river-distance and flood-zone profiles.

The measured score gain is small and does not clear the +0.0003-on-both-years bar in my own refit:
- Buildings: +0.00078 on 2024 (6 of 6 seeds) and +0.00023 out of window on 2022 (3 of 3 seeds), but -0.00009 on 2023 (2 of 6 seeds).
- Contents: +0.00031 / +0.00017, but the 2024 part comes from non-R11 rows through a spline-knot shift rather than the fix, and the critic's out-of-window results are mixed, so treat contents as zero.

Two things support testing it anyway.
- **Strong structural reason:** an unambiguous unit error in an input that every flood-related home model uses.
- **Evidence for buildings on both years:** the production predictions show a monotone R11 A/E gradient by corrected elevation, and an R11-only cross-year correction gains on both years (+0.0002 to +0.0006, k=200).

Signs against:
- The deterministic GLM components are slightly negative.
- The buildings 2023 refit is nil, within the XGBoost seed noise of about 0.0005.
- The 2024 gain rests on a few R11 claims on low ground.

Expected value is about +0.0003 on buildings and about +0.0001 pooled, with low downside: totals move by less than 0.4%. The final fit (2021-24) most resembles the 2024 window, where the gain is clearest.

Verdict: worth testing as a data correction, with no claim that it passes the two-year rule on score alone.

Scratch files, including about 107 MB of row-level prediction parquets you can delete once reviewed, are in <review scratch>/agents/verify-G1/. No repository file was touched and no pack runner was run.

(2) The data, from my own queries. Each year from 1890 to 1910 except 1900 holds 1,673 to 1,832 addresses; 1900 holds 19,014, and no other spike exists. The energy-rating mix at 1900 (A 0.14, B 0.18, C 0.18, D 0.15, E 0.13, F 0.11, G 0.09) is close to the mix of all other addresses, not to pre-1900 (F/G 0.89).
